utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Jasovic, if I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. At a look there is no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand anything. Yes, now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence; it still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Before I resume my questioning, one matter that the registry was kind enough to raise to my attention. Yesterday we admitted Prosecution Exhibit 210, and I neglect to ask that it be placed under seal and I do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 26 which was Prosecution Exhibit 210 is received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you understand me okay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, if at any time you don't understand one of my questions, please stop me and let me know and I'll try to put it more clearly. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour for this next topic I believe it appropriate to be in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I want you to look at the image in front of you. Can you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a picture of the KLA prison, or rather the house in which it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Younis if we can get a little bit closer. This, Your Honours, is actually found on page 20 of P006. Mr. Younis, could you just pan from left to right there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I would like you to just watch the screen for a moment. Now, do you recognise what you've seen on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the right-hand side was the KLA prison and on the other side was the KLA headquarters. This is the house on the right-hand side and this is the metal gate on the building where the headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, I would note that the compound on the right is labelled "Compound A," and the compound on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the left is labelled "Compound B," in the materials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right-hand side looking from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Jasovic, did you go in either of these places when you visited this site with Witness X on the 1st of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sparavalo, Witness X, the authorised officials from the Pristina SUP and I entered the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And continuing here with P005 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, could you please enter compound A.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, have a look at the image in front of you. Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Younis, I would ask you just to pan around to the left slowly so Mr. Jasovic can have a look at the entire compound. Okay. I think you can go back the way we came, please, Mr. Younis. Stop right there. Your Honours, this is the same image as page 6 of Prosecution Exhibit 6. It's labelled "building A1."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, do you recognise the building on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you visit any of the rooms inside this building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with Witness X into -- not the ground floor but the upper floor of this house where there are two rooms. Witness X told me that it was to those rooms they had taken him to interview him and to maltreat and beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, can you please lead us inside the upstairs of building A1. Go ahead and click through again there. Now, could you please turn us around so we can see this room, Mr. Younis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you recognise this place, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this -- have you ever been in this place, just for clarity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that day, the 1st of August, 1998. I entered these two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And did those rooms look any differently on the 1st of August, 1998 than you see them on the screen in front of you, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They looked different. Things were thrown around, TV sets, video recorders, and so on. Probably when the KLA staff was planning to leave this headquarters they -- there was some confusion and they took some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If Mr. Younis could click on the door to take us outside of that room. And if you could move us to the left, we'll have a look at building that is marked A2. Actually, before you -- could you go back for a moment to building A1, Mr. Younis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, did you go in any other rooms besides the two we have just seen in this building that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went left into the garage, I think, on the left-hand side where I found a sponge, and Witness X -- it was actually a foam mattress and Witness X said Safet Hyseni and Seva Petro [phoen] from Stimlje municipality who had been kidnapped had slept there. In the other part of the garage there was in my view, about -- in my estimation, that is, about 20 tonnes of flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you said "to the left." Do you mean the left part of the screen? Or please explain where you mean by "this garage."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking from the entrance through the front door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, if you could pan a little bit to the right, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, can you see that garage on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is referred to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a vehicle inside. The part above had not been built, the part above the garage, at that time I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for the record, this is garage A6. The image we see is on page 14 of P006. Mr. Younis, can you pan back to the left across the compound, please. Stop right there. For the record, this is building A2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this place. That's the other building in the same courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're currently looking at the same view as page 5 of P6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, did you go in any rooms in this building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this building, I did not enter any rooms because with Mr. X, since this was a barn, the prison and room for miscellaneous objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You mention a barn and a room for miscellaneous objects. Do you remember where those were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. Looking from the entrance to the yard on the right-hand side, the first room was a larder. Then it was a barn for cattle, for livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, I'm going to ask you to click first on the well there and pan to the left to see if we can get a --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you'll see as we go across the compound, this is another view of that same part of building A2 we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, you can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, looking at the screen in front of you, can you tell us anything about what you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part, on the left-hand side from where I sit, this was not there. But given that this picture is taken at a distance, I presume it would go for a barn I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, could you click on the next photo to the right. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic -- yeah. Mr. Younis is going to pan around this room and just look at it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record again this room is labelled A4 and you can find the same images at pages 8 and 9 of P006.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the livestock compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember if Witness X told you anything about this place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that he said that he was in the room that was meant to be a larder and that in the livestock compound that he could hear from the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, could I just remind you, be careful with the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And could we have a redaction there, Your Honours, of that name that was mentioned. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, in addition to Witness X, please be careful of mentioning other names because we're in public session. And if you have any doubts if you can say a name, ask me and we can go into private session if we have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, can you take us out of this cowshed please, and pan back to the right. Actually, before you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, the image in front of you, do you remember anything else about what you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the place in front of the cowshed where there were white caps and belts. I remember the well because we washed our hands there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could I go briefly into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, we're in open session now, so please again use care with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, can you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It slips my mind sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You have no need to apologise; don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, can you please pan to the right. And stop there. And if you could go ahead and click on the door of that room. Go ahead and go in. This is the room marked A5. You can see it, Your Honours, on pages 11, 12, and 13 of P006.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, do you recognise the place that is shown on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a larder where Person X, who had been kidnapped, was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did it look any differently on the 1st of August, 1998, than it does not image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 on the 1st of August, there was some foam mattresses here. Behind the door there was a metal bucket, which the inmates used for their number one and number two. And this is what person X told me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Younis, could you just exit and show us the courtyard again and pan a little bit to the right, please. Actually, I think we're done with P005.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, did you take anything with you when you left this place on the 1st of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: (redacted). The other caps and belts remained there. I and my colleague, Momcilo Sparavalo, did not take anything from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Without mentioning any names, if you can, do you know what happened to those caps and belts that were taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Person X who took the cap and the trouser belt?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just asking if you know. Do you know what happened to that cap and trouser belt after -- after you left this place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left that place, after we did the on-site investigation performed by authorised personnel of the Pristina SUP, I, Person X, and Momcilo Sparavalo came to the secretariat of the interior of Urosevac in Urosevac. But before that, we dropped by in the secretariat of the interior in Pristina. When we came to Urosevac, Person X and I went to the chief of the secretariat. I reported to the superior officer, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is the chief, on what we found on the crime scene. And given that Person X was apprehensive and upset, chief of the secretariat told Person X, Please calm down and take some rest and come back in two days' time to the secretariat so that the deposition could be taken for criminal charges to be instigated, given that we had to deal with a criminal -- the crime of terrorism. I came for a couple of moments with Person X to my office, and that Person X gave me the cap and the trouser belt saying that he would be returning in two days' time for them. At that time, we did not issue him with a receipt on the cap and the trouser belt. I did not depose him for criminal charges; however, Person X did not come back to the Urosevac secretariat of the interior after two days or later --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, let me just -- I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we just go briefly into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I'm going to briefly backtrack. You explained to us about your visit to this compound with Witness X. Before you came back to the SUP, did you go -- can you explain what happened right after you left that compound, if you went to any other places.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the police commander, we tried to go to Velika Stena, the crime scene, where Person X explained persons who had been kidnapped were lined into two groups, and they were taken to that spot and that they were killed there. However, when we set off from the head -- former headquarters towards Velika Stena, some hundred metres along the way we received fire from rifles opened by Siptar terrorists, the so-called KLA, and then we had to retreat. And so we did to avoid any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasovic. Now, I'm going to turn your attention back to the document we were looking at earlier, and I'm going to ask you to continue to use caution, to refer to Witness X only by that, I guess, moniker. And I'm referring to the document at tab 27, which you have in front of you. Sir, when did you type up this text?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was typed, as it can be seen in the note, on the 5th of August, 1998, with the view of expecting Person X to come so that we could depose said person to instigate a criminal investigation. But since he did not show up, on the basis of interview with him, my colleague, Momcilo Sparavalo, and at this drafted in official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can take a moment to look at the official note, if you want to, and then tell me: Is this a complete record of what Witness X told you on the 1st of August, 1998, and what you yourself saw on the visit you just described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that this is a complete record because we did not insert certain information, counting on him coming back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another document, like Prosecution Exhibit 210, that was discussed at great length during a protected witness's testimony during cross-examination and direct examination. I would move that it be admitted and given the next exhibit number under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I would be objecting to its admission based, upon other things, the witness's last answer in that the document is incomplete. It's not an accurate reflection of whatever occurred between the period of discussion between him and the witness who is unnamed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that I do. I believe that with regard to the document of yesterday, that is a document which was, if I'm not mistaken acknowledged by the witness, if I'm not mistaken. If I could have but a moment to just double-check my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean when the witness was here giving his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mean at the time that the witness was actually in fact interviewed with regard to this document. The first document -- the document of July 18th I believe -- of the July 18th interview is a document which the witness did in fact acknowledge and sign. The second document which is a document of the August documents is a document, we have heard, the witness did not acknowledge either during the witness interview. And with regard to the information that is contained in this document, we have been told it is incomplete. Now, I don't have with me the entirety of the transcript with regard to the witness's, that's Witness A's, discussion of tab 27. So I would not be in a position to argue absolutely that it wasn't covered in its entirety and I wouldn't do such a thing. However, I believe that the tab 27 information is incomplete and on that basis it should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any other submission? Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would only mention, and I think Mr. Guy-Smith corrected himself there at the end, the witness has not said that it was inaccurate, only that it was incomplete. And I would submit that during cross-examination of that protected witness and direct examination, those -- whatever information may not have been included, I think that's been fully vetted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My recollection is not complete at the moment of what occurred that -- during that cross-examination and examination. Is it your submission that this document was put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I hope Defence counsel will correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe this document was put to him by Defence counsel for Mr. Limaj, and I'm not sure if any of the other Defence counsel. He was questioned specifically about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might make a suggestion, since quite frankly my memory does not serve in specific perhaps -- ah-ha I see someone's certainly does, so I can't make this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski has been identified as well as Mr. Mansfield as culprits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe that I did and it may be for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- reason that I am standing. I'm trying to get there. If I -- if I might. Before -- if the Court would reserve ruling until I have but a moment to double-check the transcript. I'm more than happy to come back on this issue if that would be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That sounds a very practical course. We will -- if you would move on and we will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you. For this topic, I do think we have to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I'm going to ask you about a few names. I just want to see if you know these people. Do you know a person named Lutfi Xhemshiti?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally. He's a grounds-keeper from Crni Breg, from the village of Crni Breg from the Lipjan municipality. I cannot remember the exact day or month, but in 1998 he came to my office once, to my office in Urosevac, saying that while doing his rounds in the forest - he was a forester - he received death threats by so-called KLA or Siptar terrorists. And this is what I said yesterday, that those people, Albanians, who worked and served in state-owned institutions and enterprises were targeted. I met that person through the chief of the traffic police at the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac because Lutfi Xhemshiti, he served in the same barracks in the Yugoslav army with the chief of traffic police of the Urosevac SUP, but I could not say where did he performed his national service. He -- Lutfi Xhemshiti complained about these death threats to his -- to the chief of traffic police, who then referred him to me, to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, you've described one instance where Lutfi Xhemshiti came to you. Was he a police informant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that he was. I do have Siptars as colleagues to this very day, so if people socialise -- get in social contact together, that does not mean that they are informants or spies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about the -- besides social contact, what about the someone who comes and reports an incident on one occasion like this; do you consider such people police informants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior is a legal institution. Any problem ranging from a misdemeanour to a crime of course is to be reported to the nearest secretariat of interior affairs in the area where the person lives. It's a different matter that the Siptar terrorists of the so-called KLA had their scouts and they would put these spies in front of a police station, for example in Stimlje or Urosevac, to see what Siptars were coming in and out. In their view, no Siptar should, for example, apply for a licence to bear weapons, apply for an identity card, apply for a passport or any other document issued by the secretariat of the interior. Every country in Europe and in the world does the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about another name now. Did you know a person named Emin Emini? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Emin Emini. He was from the village of Crnoljevo, Stimlje municipality. I know that his wife was from the village of Racak in Stimlje municipality. I know that this was a person who was poor. He had over a hundred goats and he was kidnapped and taken to the notorious prison in Lapusnik. We also have information that his brother, whose name escapes me at the moment, was also kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was Emin Emini a police informant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the logic of the Siptar terrorists, yes; but in my view this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know a person named --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I refrained from objecting before, but at this point I'm going to object to the answer that was previously given on line 9 through 18 and being a nonresponsive to the particular question asked in its entirety. And with regard to the last answer given, I'm going to object on the grounds that it lacks a foundation and is outside of this particular witness's knowledge at this time. I believe that the question was directed towards what relationship Mr. Jasovic has with these people and whether he consider them to be police informants or not, not whether others did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question and the answer which has been asked more than once, whether somebody was a police informant, seems to have been asked on a general basis and that leaves open whether this witness can speak with authority whether there was such a status or understanding of the person in question generally in the police force rather than whether he can speak only of his own contact and dealing with the person. I think you'd better clear that up, Mr. Black, before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I will. And if Mr. Guy-Smith's objection was directed to this witness's idea of the logic of the terrorists, I'm sure Your Honours can disregard that or won't consider that as important evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, there's been a measure of evidence of such a nature yesterday and today. There have been a general forbearance which has enabled us to get along with it. But you will realise that there can be no weight attached to that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clear up the important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, over yesterday and today and I've asked you on several occasions if someone was a police informant. Did you know all of the police informants that were used by the SUP in your area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly according to the law on the interior and the rules of service in the Ministry of the Interior. If I had a registered informant, my colleague could not find out who the informant was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So when in answer to my questions you've said someone was not a police informant, was that as far as you know or was it some more broad statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the was of everything I learned. I am referring to the kidnapped persons and I am absolutely certain with reference to the persons mentioned here that they were nobody's informants or friendly contacts or anything of the kind. I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many years did you work as a policeman in this area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For six years because I know the Stimlje area very well. From the 1st of July, 1975, to the 1st of May, 1981. I was also assistant commander of the police station in Urosevac and we patrolled Stimlje together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to go back to clarify an answer that you gave before. When you said you were certain that these people weren't informants, how were you certain? Can you explain that answer any more?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Ministry of the Interior in Urosevac was dislocated to Leskovac, I found the file containing the names of the registered informants. Maybe in Urosevac I could not have had access to this information, but I did have access to it in Leskovac. Because -- because of all the other problems we had, there were two of us working on operative matters, so we kept the file at hand, the file containing the names of all the collaborators, informants, and other contacts. I don't know whether I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Black, is that a file that has been produced and disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No it hasn't, Your Honour. It's the first time I hear of such a file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the time as I understand the effect of the witness's evidence on this point, it is that he, if following the normal procedures, would keep confidential to himself who were his informants and that would not normally be known by other officers; nor would he normally know who were informants to other officers, and that the only factual basis for some different understanding may have been this book or file dealing with one of the stations, a file we haven't had disclosed. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that's generally correct, Your Honour. I would say this one station was the headquarters for the entire area, and I believe he -- his first response when I asked him about this question was that he is basing this assessment on all the things that he learned as a police officer in this area during the years that he mentioned as well as this list that he has now said that he saw after leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're basing it generally. You get no further than the general position, do you not, that one officer normally would not know who was an informant of another officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wish I had been more specific in this. What I've been driving at is whether, as far as he knew, any of these people were police informants. If you think I need to explore that more, I am happy to do so, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have given you my indication of what my impression is of the effect of the evidence on this point so far. If you want to try and make more on it, please go ahead; if Mr. Guy-Smith wants to make more of it, he will have a full opportunity. But we have got some factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I have a moment to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the conference is going on, may I raise one point and that is: It would be useful to know whether the register exists because in fact it's not the first time he mentioned it; he mentioned it yesterday in relation to informants. And it would be useful to know whether it exists, whether he means the register in relation to his particular informant or whether he means a general register on which his informant appeared along with a lot of other people, which is the one he may now be talking about. But if he's going to be giving evidence which is based on either of those two registers, we would be grateful to know if they exist, and if they do where they are, and whether there's any possibility of any access to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that submission effectively interrupted the discussion on the other side of the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate the indulgence. I'll do my best to try to explore this issue a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you've mentioned this register, this file. Does that still exist?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it does, in the secretariat of interior affairs in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that a document that the Tribunal could have access to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You must ask a higher authority because this is a strictly confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what higher authority should be contacted if we were to make such a request or if the Defence were to make such a request?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't fall within my competence. It's the job of the chief of the secretariat of Urosevac, and he would certainly be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, in addition to registered contacts, you said that you were certain these people were not friendly contacts. On what basis did you make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I believe in your testimony and in a recent -- in an answer you gave a few minutes ago you said you were certain these people were not registered contacts or friendly contacts. And I've asked you a couple of questions about the registered, but now I want to focus on friendly contacts. How did you know that these men were not friendly -- friendly contacts of the police or police informants in that sense, non-registered informants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify this, a friendly contact is not the same as a registered contact. It's a person who comes to the offices of their own accord or to a special place to provide some information of interest to the service. This operative contact is not registered. Let me clarify. Only collaborators and informants are registered. There are also operative contacts, friendly contacts, and so on. I don't know how clear I've been. A collaborator must be told he is providing information of interest to the service. Another kind of contact need not be told this. He doesn't even have to know it. I don't know how clear I've been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know about the friendly contacts of your colleagues, who they were, those friendly contacts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know and I wasn't interested in their contacts. Every country -- in every country of the world, no colleague will tell another who his friendly contacts are and you don't ask whose collaborators -- or who the collaborators or informants or friendly or operative contacts are of a colleague. If a colleague submits an official note relating to terrorism and submits it to our superior, it might be delivered to me in the line of work, but the information might have been provided -- he might say the information is provided by a registered contact. But that need not be the case. He might be providing information given him by a friendly contact. A collaborator, informant, friendly connection, or operative connection must be protected so that that person or their family do not suffer any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, given what you've just explained to us, on what basis are you certain that these people were not friendly contacts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I didn't say they were not friends; I'm saying they were not registered contacts. In other words, that they are not a collaborator or an informant who must be registered. That's what I'm saying. Friendly contacts are something quite different. I might have a friend who is a Siptar, and while we are sitting in a cafe or somewhere he might give me a piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an appropriate time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you need to add something more, Mr. Jasovic, please go ahead and do so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say: Nobody would ask a colleague who their contacts were, whether registered or unregistered, because you could use either registered or unregistered contacts. But a colleague proposing someone to our superior might want to register that person, either as a collaborator or as an informant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, then -- now, just focusing on yourself and not on your colleagues, were any of these people that we've talked about, the names were Agim Ademi, Shyqyri Zymeri, Vesel Ahmeti, Adem Ramadani, Shefqet Ramadani, were any of these men registered contacts or friendly contacts for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the person I mentioned yesterday, none of these were registered with me, none of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you say "apart from the person I mentioned yesterday," is that the the person you referred to yesterday as a registered contact? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I was referring to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you said "none of these were registered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with me." But were they unregistered informants? Were they friendly contacts for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not my friendly contacts. With some of them I did sit in a cafe. That's where we could sit together. It doesn't mean that he's a friendly contact. He might be a friend. According to the rules of the service of friendly contact is something else. It's a different matter if I sit down in a cafe or somewhere else with a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Explain the difference between a friendly contact and a friend, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have many Siptars who are friends of mine. I never asked a friend of mine for any official information. However, a friend might enter the offices and give us official information; that's not impossible. I don't know how to explain this. A friendly contact is a friend who gives you information. But I would never abuse my friends because I could get information from other people. I wanted to keep my friends as friends, and I also wanted to keep my registered contacts. I never forced a friend of mine to give me information, only if he volunteered and came into the police station to report a crime or a misdemeanour or to tell us who a possible perpetrator might be of a crime. How can I explain this? The -- I don't think even the person who drew up the rules of service could explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Jasovic. I think you've done your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, do you know Xheladin Ademaj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know him back when I used to work as a policeman at the Stimlje police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what he does for a living?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His profession is miller. I got to know him while I was a policeman patrolling in the Petrovo village and other villages, and I visited him in his home in Petrovo through my colleagues of Albanian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with him in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I could not say exactly, but I believe that from the end of 1997 I did not -- did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you learn about anything that happened to him in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that he was kidnapped and forcibly removed by members of the so-called KLA and that he was taken to Lapusnik camp. I found out in the first half of July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you learn anything about his fate, about what happened to him after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the Lapusnik camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. After he -- any time after he was kidnapped. Do you know what happened to him after he was kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the kidnapping he was taken to the Lapusnik prison. I learned but I cannot recall how he managed to get away when they were lined in 1998 and they were taken to Velika Stena. I don't know how he managed to stay alive. I was contacted after the 25th of July. My colleague contacted him over the phone, Srboljub Vojinovic. He told me -- he said, Xheladin Ademaj contacted me from Switzerland, told me that he was safe and sound. I asked that colleague whether he explained any circumstances surrounding his kidnapping, but he said he was not supposed to say. He was afraid and allegedly that telephone was tapped. I'm telling you this on the basis what I heard from my colleague, Srboljub Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As far as you personally know, Mr. Jasovic, was Xheladin Ademaj ever a police informant or a police contact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- he was not my registered informant. I can tell you that neither was he an informant of my other colleagues. He is known because he -- most of the Serbs used to buy flour from Xheladin Ademaj, from his mill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last thing I want to have you look at is the document behind tab 11 in the binder that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: For the record, this bears the ERN K032-7360. It's a supplementary statement, the 25th [sic] of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, have a look at this, and when you're done tell me who took this statement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague, Momcilo Sparavalo, and I took that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we go briefly into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, if you could follow along and I'm going to read a paragraph that's halfway down the page in the B/C/S version. I want to see if this is an accurate recollection of what was given to you. It says: "When the terrorist actions were being committed against police and army members in the section of the main road between villages" -- and then it's illegible.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Village of Belince.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what were the villages that you just mentioned, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Belince, Stimlje municipality, to above the village of Crnoljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll continue. It says: "Terrorists from the area of Lapusnik and Malisevo - led by Commander Celik who is in Malisevo - came to the aid of terrorist I mentioned in previous statement. I heard that Celik was in the company of a former policeman from Racak village with the pseudonym of Qerqiz who had some kind of higher function in the so-called KLA. I also know that the terrorists from Lapusnik were trained to use sniper rifles and hand-held launchers. The persons with the nickname Celiku was the commander of the so-called KLA in the area between Lapusnik and Urosevac." Mr. Jasovic, my question for you is: Did you receive that from information from the person we just mentioned in private session?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasovic. You can close the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for the moment, Your Honour, I think I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The only thing, Your Honour, is I don't know if it would be a proper time to go back to the issue of tab 27 so it can be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will receive a Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 27 would be Prosecution Exhibit 211, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're up and ready to run, Mr. Topolski, in more sense than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour's information is as good as mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It probably has the same source. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asked -- I've asked to go first and my learned friends have very kindly agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I represent, together with Mr. Powles, who sits next to me here, Isak Musliu. Do you think that the word "Siptar" is offensive to Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In primary and secondary school, I used to be taught Siptar language and I noticed over the TV when former Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, when Palma Plus, that's a TV station situated in Jagodina interviewed him, he said "Une jam Siptar." In translation that means "I'm a Siptar." To me, my opinion is this is not a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Isn't it the equivalent of calling a black man a nigger?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. I was born in Kosova in Metohija. I was not born elsewhere, so I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I would be very grateful on behalf of the client I represent, who takes the very deepest offence to that word, if you were not to use it again. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you understand me? I'm asking you not to use that word again. You smile, Mr. Jasovic. Is this amusing in some way for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the starting point of Milosevic's political agenda in the late 1980s was the restoration of Serbian control over Kosova? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not a politician. I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You are a loyal Serb; yes, you can answer this question. You agree with that, don't you? That was the Milosevic agenda and you agreed with it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not a politician. I don't know how to answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Truthfully would be a start, Mr. Jasovic. This was about regaining Serbian control of Kosova, wasn't it? That was the agenda of Milosevic, that's what brought him to power, and you were a Milosevic supporter, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- as I said, I'm not a politician. I respected the laws and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and I performed my duties in accordance with the constitution and laws, in accordance with the law on internal affairs, the interior ministry, and in accordance with the rules of service of the MUP of Republic of Serbia. I'm just performer of duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So you are a performer of duties and a respecter of the law and constitution of the Republic of Serbia. Is that your evidence, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that I worked in accordance with the laws and constitution of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I mean you broke the law more than you observed it, Mr. Jasovic; that's what I mean. Do you agree with me or do you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct that I broke the law. I worked in accordance with the laws of Serbia and the constitution, pursuant to the law on the Ministry of the Interior and the rules of service of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps what you are able to agree with me about because you were there is that after March of 1998 in Kosova, the battle really, once the KLA started to emerge, the battle was to restore Serb control, wasn't it? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You could not agree with me. Well, let's see if you can agree with this: My suggestion is that Belgrade and all its agents, and you were one of them, used the pretext of fighting the insurgency of the KLA to begin a new campaign of ethnic cleansing in Kosova. You were part of a machine whose aim it was to cleanse Kosova of Kosovan Albanians. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree and this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You and your colleagues I suggest, Sparavalo in particular, Vojinovic and your men were part of Belgrade's policy and process to ethnically cleanse Kosova. That is what you were about in 1998, and before and after it, I suggest. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree because this is not correct. I already said that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I worked in accordance with the laws and constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggest that you and your colleague -- colleagues and the men under you intimidated innocent civilians. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree because I could not intimidate anybody. I worked in an office of the secretariat of the interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggest that you and your colleagues mistreated innocent members of the Albanian community. Do you agree or to you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. It is up to you to have your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't hold opinions; I put a case. I suggest you tortured innocent members of the Albanian community. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggest you murdered members of the Albanian community, you and your colleagues. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put it to you that we did not kill Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suggest to your face, as I suggested about you many months ago from this very position I stand in now: You were a butcher. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was the SUP part of the Serbian state machine? Do you agree with that at least?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my remit and as regards this question, you should address this question to the chief of the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that David Gajic, the person you've just referred to, the chief of the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time chief -- you mean in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac was Bogoljub Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you. You worked for it. Was SUP part of the Serbian state machine, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, truthfully, Mr. Jasovic, would be a start. You worked for it. You were a member of it. You were a commander in it. Was it part of the state machine? You do understand what I mean by that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, my remit was to work in accordance with the laws and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, pursuant to the law of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and in accordance with the rules of service of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators of this Tribunal, you indicated that one area of your work came under the heading of political delinquency. What's that, political delinquency, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the orders of the senior officer, the chief of the secretariat, together with colleagues from state security, I worked on tasks concerning the establishment of KLA staffs or headquarters on identifying the top brass of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Doesn't political delinquency mean that you treated as an enemy everyone who didn't agree with you? Isn't that what it means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Certainly. A political delinquent is someone who doesn't agree with the Serbian view of the world? That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Political delinquent, in my opinion, is a person who kidnaps people, maltreats, tortures people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In your statement to the ICTY, paragraph 5 of it, you say this: "Following the protest in 1989 and 1990, the Albanian population demanded independence. The Albanians demanded their own constitution and refused to go to school and work under the laws of the Republic of Serbia. As a result of this, most of the Albanians gave up their positions, not only in the Police, but also in other working places." Is it your serious and honest evidence that Albanians simply walked away voluntarily from their jobs or were they rather forced out, Mr. Jasovic? Which is the truth of it would you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is this: I will start, sir, with the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac. We begged our colleagues to remain in their posts, and in all these circumstances, some of them remained in service, continuing with their tasks and their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What about the teachers, doctors, people like that? Did they just walk away from their jobs? Did they just walk out or were they forced out? Students from universities who couldn't complete degrees, did they just walk away, Mr. Jasovic, or were you and your colleagues forcing them out by your treatment of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior is not in charge of forcing anybody out of their job. We never did that and we would never do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's a lie, I suggest. That is a simple lie. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that it is true that Albanians were not forced out of their jobs. I -- when it comes to the education system, I cannot recall correctly. There were three or four contentious cases, because those holding those jobs did not want to accept the curriculum of the Republic of Serbia. They continued working under the Kosovo curriculum. I'm not a politician. I don't know how to continue explaining this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's get to an area where you're a bit more comfortable or at home. If you're not at home in politics, let's talk about informers. Now, being in the position you were in in the 1980s and 1990s, you, of course, were working in the field, as you would describe it, of counter-terrorism. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the end of 1989 and the beginning of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And onwards, and once the KLA emerged in the late 1980s. There was counter-terrorism you were dealing with, wasn't it, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Yesterday I pointed out that together with a colleague, an Albanian, I was in charge of the line of work dealing with interethnic conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And then you got involved in the line of work dealing with the KLA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to orders -- pursuant to orders from the chief of the secretariat together with the state security service I worked on the tasks I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Which included the KLA, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The KLA, as far as you were concerned, were a bunch of criminals, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, the KLA was an illegal terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Criminals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify this? A criminal can be a burglar or a pickpocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, try and take where you're sitting seriously for a moment, will you? You know exactly what I mean. You regarded the KLA as a bunch of criminals. Counter-revolutionaries. That's what they were, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When KLA staffs were established, they were all established with a view to carrying out terrorist activities against members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, the Army of Yugoslavia. And as I said yesterday, they dealt very harshly with loyal Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's -- sorry. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Albanians who were working in state-owned enterprises and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's focus for a moment or two on some of this terminology you use. Loyal Albanians and cooperative Albanians. You used the word "cooperative Albanians" in your statement. Sparavalo, who made a statement to this Tribunal, used the word "loyal Albanians." Does that mean the same thing to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, a loyal Albanian is an Albanian who did not oppose the law and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, but rather respected the law and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did the world eventually respect the law and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Jasovic? I have in mind March 1999 when the bombs started to drop.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No. Let's talk about another distinction that you draw when you're dealing with informers between a friendly connection and an operative connection. Do I understand you to be saying that a friendly connection is somebody who came in themselves voluntarily to give you information? Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, a friendly contact or connection is a person I associated with or socialised with. And a friendly contact, for example, while we were socialising said to me, I have heard about such-and-such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yesterday you distinguished such a person from somebody who you called an operative connection - and it's page 26, line 11 of the unrevised transcript - when you said this: "An operative connection can be a source who a not registered, a person to whom I give specific assignments." So do I understand you to be saying, Mr. Jasovic, that an operative connection is someone you send out to do your dirty work for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operative connection is a person who is not a registered contact; he is not sent out on to the field. But -- he is not linked to investigating a particular crime. He is given a specific task or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: He is linked to investigating a particular crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he is given a specific task to help discover the perpetrators of a particular crime. And this is not a registered contact because all contacts -- well, it wasn't only Serbs who used contacts. Every country in the world uses contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you send people out into the community to commit crime in order to inform on others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you find that funny, Mr. Jasovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Or is your laughter the laughter of embarrassment because you did do such a thing and you wouldn't have the courage now to admit it, would you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not embarrassed. I carried out my duties conscientiously and properly and in accordance -- and honourably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can -- sorry, I didn't want to interrupt you. Did you want to say something else? Did you want to add to the list of adjectives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conscientiously, honestly and honourably. That's how all my colleagues worked as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Conscientiously, honestly and honourably. Did you and your colleagues on the morning of April 11, 1994 conscientiously, honestly and properly attach electrodes to an 18-year-old and electrocute him in Urosevac police station? Did you do that, honestly, conscientiously and properly, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, you need a date for this, do you? Well, the date, Mr. Jasovic, is the 11th of April of 1994. The initials of the boy concerned were F. E., and he lived with his mother and his younger brothers. "They ordered me to take off my pants" -- listen to me, please, then you can answer. "So they pulled them off. They tied my hands behind my back with my belt. The one held down my head. The other sat on my legs. They stacked wires from that apparatus that looked like a phone in my ears and on my sex organs. The pain was horrible." The 11th of April, 1994. Was that you and your colleagues conscientiously, honourably, and properly carrying out your duty for the Serb state, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of April, 1998, the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac was dislocated to certain houses and places. It is not correct that physical force or other forms of torture were used against this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. The date I put the 11th of April, 1994. Not 8, 4. Do you want to change your answer now? Pardon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't happen in 1994 either, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Such a thing -- such a thing Dragan Jasovic would have no part of. Is that your evidence, Mr. Jasovic? I want to be clear about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never participate in dirty work and I would never overstep the boundaries of my authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We shall see some examples of people who have sworn statements to this Tribunal that you did just that, Mr. Jasovic. And I'll come back to it. I wonder if I could draw a distinction between friendly and operative connections of yours. Isn't the difference really and in reality between those who volunteer to come in and see you and those you drag in off the streets, torture and force to work for you? Isn't that the difference?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never forced anyone to give any kind of information. For me, that would not be good information; it would be incorrect information if it was given under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's what I suggested at the beginning, really, Mr. Jasovic. This was only part of it, this information-gathering pretext. The point was that you were about intimidating and terrifying and getting rid of Albanians. One of the ways to do it was to behave in the way you and your colleagues did. Ethnic cleansing by any other name, Mr. Jasovic. That's what I suggest you were about. You disagree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it a mere coincidence that your one and only named registered source between 1986 and 1998 is dead? Is it really your evidence you only had one in all those years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's true evidence, is it, one registered informant in 12 years of policing, and he's dead so we can't ask him anything, you see. That's the point. Just one, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one registered informant; that's true. Not in 12 years of service, but a full 30 years of effective service as of the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: One registered informant in 30 years of effective service. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you just have tab 17, please, in front of you. Turn that up. We're not going to look at the content; it's just that I want to use it as a jumping-off point for a question. Just have it in front of you for convenience's sake. You spoke about this yesterday and you told us yesterday that the four people who are mentioned as the statement-takers were yourself, Sparavalo, Janicevic and Antic. Do you remember telling us about this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that we took this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. And because is it that I --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that we took the statement, Momcilo Sparavalo, Srboljub Vojinovic, Miroslav Antic and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Because I make the suggestion to you loudly and clearly, I hope, for you to understand, Mr. Jasovic, that you in SUP were all part of the state machine. Do I understand you to say yesterday that you and Sparavalo were from public security and the other two gentlemen were from state security. Is the evidence you gave us yesterday, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that yesterday and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So, it would be fair to say in general terms, wouldn't it, Mr. Jasovic, that as an outsider looking in on this situation here, that really what you're doing is public and state security, working together hand in hand with Belgrade. Would you agree with that? In general terms, would that be a fair description of the situation you were in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public and state security cooperated in Urosevac; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And under the umbrella, the overall leadership and, I would suggest, guidance of Belgrade and the Serb authorities there. Would you agree with that? In general terms, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Belgrade, I don't know. As I said, I was only a performer of duties. I was a crime policeman, an inspector. And with respect to this question, you can ask my superiors, the chief of the Urosevac public security station, Bogoljub Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you were just following orders, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working according to the law and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did all my work pursuant to orders from the chief of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's just consider for a moment or two together your statement-taking procedures. You told us yesterday, transcript page 10, line 10, and I quote you: "I had my own method of work." Do you remember telling us that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Does that involve having a gun on the desk and sticks in the corner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't wear a pistol. I don't carry one and I didn't carry it then either. I did not have a truncheon because it's uniformed policemen who carry truncheons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's bigger than a truncheon what I had in mind. I'm recollecting what a witness told us a few weeks ago from that very chair. "Big stick in the corner and all that Jasovic has to do is just point to it. That's enough." Did you have that in the corner of your desk, of your room, Mr. Jasovic? A stick?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. I don't remember having any kind of stick there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it a coincidence that the phrase "so-called KLA" keeps occurring in all of the witness statements that you take and it's your phrase that you use to describe the KLA, "the so-called KLA?" Is that phrase repeating itself a mere coincidence, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The so-called KLA" is an expression that is used because it was not a legal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder why a farmer from the Albanian Kosovan countryside would use the phrase "so-called KLA" in a statement made to you, unless of course you were putting the words in his mouth. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who made statements used that expression. I can say it was not a real army; it was a so-called army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's what it means. Very well. Mr. Jasovic, I suggest that you had then and you have now a pathological hatred of all things Albanian. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree because I have relatives, family connections with persons of Albanian ethnic origin. And I am not capable of hating anyone, whether Albanian or Macedonian or Slovenian, or English for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Some of your best friends are Albanian. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I still have several friends who call me on the phone nearly every day from Skopje, from Urosevac, from Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's examine together --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kacanik and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's examine together for a few moments if we may, please, whether there is any substance in this firm suggestion that I have made that you have a pathological hatred of Albanians, did then, and do now. I want to look at what I suggest is some manifestations of that hatred in action. First of all, are you aware of an organisation in your home country called the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where is the headquarters? I have heard about certain humanitarian organisations but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Pristina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware that -- or you may not be if you haven't heard of the organisation. Have you ever heard of the fact that that organisation, a legitimate and proper organisation, I suggest, has reported into the activities of police stations during -- before and during the war and the stations you worked at are included in that report. Are you heard about such a document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You haven't.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Ferizaj, Urosevac, is a place where you worked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Urosevac, not Orahovac. I was there only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Between 1991 and 1999, this organisation has come across, supported by medical evidence, 449 victims of torture, of which 371 of them, 82 per cent, passed through your police station when you were serving there. Would you care to comment, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. These persons did not pass through my office, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
